module_title: Network Topologies (Star, Ring, Mesh, Bus) - Structural Layouts
introduction: This intermediate tier transitions from geographical span to physical design. 'Topology' refers to the geometric arrangement or physical layout of how computers (Nodes) and cables are connected to each other in a network. SSC and Banking exams heavily test the advantages and points of failure for each layout.

core_concepts.title: Bus Topology
core_concepts.description:
All computers are connected to a single, continuous central cable known as the 'Backbone'. Data travels linearly along this cable. 
Failure Point: If the central backbone cable breaks, the entire network immediately collapses.

core_concepts.title: Star Topology
core_concepts.description:
The most widely used topology in the world. Every single computer is connected individually to a central hardware device called a 'Hub' or 'Switch'. 
Advantage: If one computer's cable breaks, the rest of the network keeps working perfectly. 
Failure Point: If the central Hub/Switch fails, the entire network goes down.

core_concepts.title: Ring Topology
core_concepts.description:
Computers are connected in a closed-loop circle. Data travels strictly in one direction (unidirectional) from one computer to the next until it reaches its destination. 
Failure Point: If a single computer crashes or one cable breaks, the circular data flow is interrupted, causing a complete network failure.

core_concepts.title: Mesh Topology
core_concepts.description:
Every single computer is connected directly to EVERY OTHER computer in the network via dedicated cables. 
Advantage: It is highly 'Fault-Tolerant' and the most secure. If one cable breaks, data just takes another route. 
Disadvantage: It is extremely expensive and complex to wire.

important_entities.name: Node
important_entities.significance: In networking terminology, a 'Node' is any physical device attached to the network that can send or receive data (e.g., a computer, a printer, or a scanner).

important_entities.name: Terminator
important_entities.significance: Hardware devices placed at both extreme ends of a 'Bus Topology' backbone cable. They absorb data signals so the signal doesn't bounce back and cause data collisions.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: Most Reliable vs. Most Common Trap
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A classic examiner trap! If asked 'Which topology is the most secure and reliable?', the answer is strictly 'Mesh'. However, if asked 'Which topology is the most commonly used in practical life?', the answer is 'Star'.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: A Mesh is a Mess of wires
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Remember that 'Mesh' has the highest amount of physical cabling because every device has a dedicated wire going to every other device, creating a massive web/mess of cables.

exam_strategy_tips: Always associate the term 'Hub' or 'Switch' exclusively with the 'Star Topology'. If a question mentions a central device failing, they are testing the Star topology.
